title: Kappa's island (Sn 5)
hookLine: read it: for those in the flood, an island: owning nothing, grasping nothing
tomorrow: how does a busy mind ever go still? a student asks it straight.

cards: News footage of a flood: water to the windowsills, and one roof, one patch of high ground, with people standing on it, waiting. Nobody up there is talking about the furniture anymore. A student named Kappa asks for that.
For those standing in the middle of the stream, he says, swept by aging and death, tell me an island. The answer fits in one breath, and Buddhists read it in two ways.

teach.b: Here's the Buddha's answer to Kappa. Owning nothing, grasping nothing: this is the island, and there is no other. I call it nibbana, the end of aging and death.
Those who know this, mindful and at peace here and now, don't fall under the sway of Mara, the tempter. So, the debate. One reading takes owning nothing at its word.
This is the voice of the monastic life: monks and nuns keep a robe and a bowl and live on what's given.

Their best case: the hand that holds little finds it easier not to grasp. Owning nothing outwardly keeps the inner letting go honest. You can't fool yourself about clinging when there's almost nothing to cling to.

The other reading, voiced by lay teachers and householders, puts the weight on grasping nothing. Their best case: the Buddha taught kings, merchants and parents too, and gave them advice on handling wealth well.
The flood is craving, not furniture. A person with a house and a family can hold it all with an open hand, and that open hand is the island. Notice what both readings keep.
Neither says the island is a place you get to someday.
Both say it's here and now, wherever grasping stops.
And both put the two halves together: owning nothing, grasping nothing. They argue about which half carries the weight.

how: Buddhist monks and nuns keep few possessions and live on alms; lay Buddhists practice generosity and non-clinging within family and working life. Both draw on lines like Kappa's island.

o: the boat a student used to cross over to the Buddha
an island in the flood: owning nothing, grasping nothing
a real island where a student built a hut to meditate

p: own little, and grasping gets honest
the flood is craving, not furniture

s: the Buddha's island is a place you reach only after death
the poem says those who know it are at peace here and now.
Buddhists read 'owning nothing, grasping nothing' with different weight
monastic voices stress owning little; lay voices stress the open hand.

games.q: you read the island as inner: grasp nothing, own what you need. a friend who's training as a nun reads it literally. what's her best case?
o: holding little keeps you honest; there's almost nothing left to cling to.
owning things is wrong in itself, so all property has to go.
the Buddha forbade lay people from owning anything at all.
games.why: that's the monastic reading at its strongest. the lay reading has its own: the flood is craving, and an open hand can hold a home. the poem keeps both halves.

practice: Pick up one thing near you that you could live without: a pen, a mug, a spare charger. Hold it in an open palm, not a fist.
You don't have to give it away; just rest with it in the open hand and feel what owning it lightly is like, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Kappa's island: for those caught midstream, with the water rising, the Buddha names one island and says there is no other. Owning nothing, grasping nothing, the end of aging and death, here and now.

orig.note: Pali: island. Owning nothing, grasping nothing: this is the dipa.

carryVoice: Somewhere dry to stand, even midstream: the island, wherever the grip lets go. Sixteen seventy-six, high ground.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 5.11 (Kappamanavapuccha, Kappa's question, in the Parayanavagga)
